Spy turned startup CEO: 'The WannaCry of AI will happen'

AI + ML

Ah, the good old days when 0-day development took a year

INTERVIEW "In my past life, it would take us 360 days to develop an amazing zero day," Zafran Security CEO Sanaz Yashar said.

She's talking about the 15 years she spent working as a spy - she prefers "hacking architect" - inside the Israel Defense Forces' elite cyber group, Unit 8200.

"Now, the volume and speed is changing so much that for the first time ever, we have a negative time-to-exploit, meaning it takes less than a day to see vulnerabilities being exploited, being weaponized before they were patched," Yashar told The Register. "That is not something you used to see."

The reason: AI. This technology isn't helping criminals develop novel or more sophisticated attack chains entirely without humans in the loop, she said. "But AI is helping the threat actors do more, and faster," according to Yashar - and the more and faster is what worries her.

As a teen, Yashar's family moved from Tehran to Israel, and the Israeli military intelligence corps recruited her while she was working as a research assistant at Tel Aviv University.

In 2022, Yashar co-founded Zafran, which uses AI to help companies map and manage their cyber-threat exposure. But before heading up her own security startup, she led threat intelligence at Cybereason and worked as a manager at Google's incident response and threat intel biz, Mandiant.

Unified Action Systems Critical to Reducing Cyber Risk

# Unified Action Systems Critical to Reducing Cyber Risk

Zafran Security's Sanaz Yashar on Proactive Threat Exposure Management Michael Novinson (MichaelNovinson) • June 20, 2025 

Sanaz Yashar, co-founder and CEO, Zafran Security

Attackers' speed and scale has put cyber defenders on unprecedented footing. Zero-day exploits are no longer rare anomalies but fast-moving weapons increasingly discovered by artificial intelligence, said Sanaz Yashar, co-founder and CEO, Zafran Security.

Nation-state actors escalate tensions with stealthy persistence, using legitimate company tools to avoid detection. In this environment, reactive security models fall short. Yashar called for building integrated systems of insights and actions. Isolated security tools that fail to communicate contribute to risk.

"Not everything is insight," she said. "The system of action is an aggregated view of what's the easiest and safest thing you can do to protect the vulnerable asset."

In this video interview with Information Security Media Group at Gartner Security & Risk Management Summit, Yashar also discussed:

- Why security must be proactive, not reactive;
- Why tools should integrate detection and remediation;
- The need for cultural change for sustained defense.

# “There is no B-2 bomber in cyber”: Iranian-born Israeli CEO warns of Tehran’s digital pivot

## Zafran Security’s Sanaz Yashar, a Unit 8200 veteran born in Tehran, says Iran’s shifting tactics favor cyber operations that are fast, covert, and aimed at regime legitimacy.

20:21, 23.06.25 

As the conflict between Iran and Israel grinds on and Tehran’s nuclear ambitions face new setbacks, a new front is rapidly emerging - one that operates in silence, across invisible battle lines. According to Sanaz Yashar, an Iranian-born Israeli cyber expert and the CEO of Zafran Security, Iran is shifting its focus to cyber warfare not just out of necessity, but as a calculated strategic move.

“I think that now that the nuclear ambitions of Iran have been delayed, they could retaliate in two different levels,” Yashar told CNBC on Monday. “First, the tactical level would be to impact the economy of the U.S.”
